mcqs.question: You open browser DevTools' Elements panel on a page that ran JavaScript after load. Why might it look different from the page's raw HTML source (view-source)?
options: DevTools decodes character entities that view-source leaves raw
view-source always shows an older, cached copy of the page
The Elements panel strips out script tags automatically
DevTools shows the live DOM, which JavaScript may have mutated since the HTML was first parsed
mcqs.explanation: view-source shows the original response bytes; the Elements panel serializes the current, live DOM, which can diverge arbitrarily once scripts add, remove, or rewrite nodes. Entity decoding and script stripping aren't what causes the divergence.

mcqs.question: Why can't the CSSOM be built incrementally the same streaming way the DOM is?
options: CSS files are always small enough that streaming wouldn't help anyway
Because a later rule in the same stylesheet can override an earlier one, so the whole stylesheet must be parsed before final values are known
Because CSSOM nodes require a fully completed DOM to attach to
Because browsers intentionally serialize CSS parsing to reduce CPU usage
mcqs.explanation: Cascade resolution needs the complete rule set because a rule appearing later can still win, so committing to a value before the stylesheet finishes parsing could be wrong. The CSSOM and DOM are built independently of each other, not sequentially dependent.

options: Scripts are simply larger files than images on average
Only script tags trigger the preload scanner to run
Browsers block on scripts specifically to enforce the same-origin policy
A script can call document.write or mutate the DOM the parser is still building, so the parser can't safely continue past it without waiting
mcqs.explanation: Scripts can rewrite the very document the parser is constructing, so the browser has to pause and let the script finish before trusting the tree's state. File size, the preload scanner, and same-origin policy aren't what forces the block.

mcqs.question: You have two independent analytics scripts with no dependency on each other or on DOM-ready state. Which loading attribute fits best, and why?
options: async — execution order doesn't matter here, and it avoids blocking parsing while downloading
defer — it guarantees a specific execution order these scripts don't actually need
Neither — plain <script> is safest since blocking always guarantees correctness
async — because it blocks parsing until the download completes, ensuring reliability
mcqs.explanation: async downloads without blocking the parser and executes whenever the download finishes, in completion order — exactly right when scripts are independent of each other. defer's ordering guarantee is unnecessary overhead here, and plain script would needlessly block parsing.

mcqs.question: A loop reads el.offsetHeight immediately after writing el.style.width, for many elements, and profiling shows repeated forced synchronous layout. What's the fix?
options: Wrap the loop in a try/catch to suppress the layout warnings
Separate all the writes from all the reads into two passes, or batch them with requestAnimationFrame
Replace offsetHeight reads with a CSS custom property instead
Move the loop's execution into a Web Worker
mcqs.explanation: Layout thrashing comes from interleaving layout-invalidating writes with layout-dependent reads; separating the two phases lets the browser batch layout once instead of recomputing it per element. A Web Worker can't touch the DOM at all, and CSS variables don't avoid the read.
